summary: Describes the Common Indexing Protocol framework: its architecture and how servers exchange indices of the information they hold, so searches can be directed to the right place.

plainLanguage.summary: The Common Indexing Protocol (CIP) lets servers share summaries of the data they hold, so that a later search can be sent to the server most likely to have the answer. Only servers speak CIP. Clients keep using the data access protocol they already know, such as LDAP or HTTP, and receive a referral when the server that answers them thinks the answer lies elsewhere.

subtitle: A framework for servers to pass indexing information, so a later search reaches the dataset most likely to hold the answer.

tldr.problem: Without indexing information a server can only answer from its own dataset, so a distributed search has to be replicated to every sub-dataset, which wastes network and server resources.
tldr.mechanism: Servers pass index objects to each other in a mesh. Each object has a header naming the index type, the dataset it describes and a base URI, plus a payload holding the index. A server uses the indices it holds to send the client a referral to the dataset most likely to hold the answer.
tldr.outcome: The result is a backend protocol in which servers keep their own data access protocol for clients while indices travel separately, so a query can be aimed at one dataset instead of broadcast. This document is one of three: RFC 2652 defines the MIME objects and RFC 2653 the transports.

facts.label: Transports named
facts.value: TCP connections and Internet mail messages

today: RFC 2651 is a Proposed Standard from August 1999 and is neither obsoleted nor updated. It is the framework document of the CIP family: RFC 2652 defines the MIME objects and RFC 2653 the transport systems. The text itself points to the Whois++ mesh documents, RFC 1913 and RFC 1914, for the mesh traversal algorithm it reuses and for the POLLED-BY and POLLED-FOR commands it mentions.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 2651 describes the Common Indexing Protocol (CIP), a framework for passing indexing information from one server to another so that a later client query can be directed to the right place. Query routing is the process of redirecting and replicating queries through a distributed database system towards the servers holding the desired results.

CIP is a backend protocol: it is spoken only between servers. Those same servers also speak a data access protocol such as LDAP, Whois++, HTTP or Z39.50 to serve clients, and they use the indexing information that CIP collected to decide where to send each query.

The document is one of three. This one covers the fundamental concepts and framework of CIP. RFC 2652 describes the MIME objects that make up the items passed by the transport system, RFC 2653 gives requirements and examples for the transport systems, and a second set of documents describes the specifications for specific index types.

CIP grew out of the Whois++ directory service, defined in RFC 1913 and RFC 1914, where indexing was tied to a single index object type called the centroid. This specification describes CIP version 3, a major overhaul of the protocol, and version 3 servers can interoperate with earlier servers in an index-passing mesh through a short negotiation sequence.
sections.plainLanguage: CIP lets servers share summaries of the data they hold, so a later search can be sent to the server most likely to have the answer. Only servers speak it. Clients keep using the data access protocol they already know, such as LDAP or HTTP, and get a referral when the server that answers them thinks the answer lies elsewhere.

sections.title: Query Routing in a Distributed Database
sections.content:
Each server handles queries over a fixed domain of data, which this RFC calls the dataset. Clients search a dataset and retrieve parts of it through a data access protocol, and each protocol suits the kind of data it was designed for.

Without indexing, a server can answer only from its own dataset. When a server holds indexing information collected from peers, it can also answer on the strength of external indices, and it can reply with a referral that points to another dataset. An index is not a copy of the remote dataset but a reduced form of it, so a referral is a hint about where to look rather than a promise of a match.

Query routing is the act of moving a query closer to the datasets that can satisfy it. In some distributed systems every query is replicated to every sub-dataset, which wastes network and server resources and is sometimes disabled outright; indexing opens the door to more efficient distributed searching.

It stays the client's job to collate, filter and follow the referrals it receives, which gives the end user, or an agent taking the user's place, the greatest control over how the query is resolved. A proxy can also resolve referrals on the client's behalf, so that a simple client can still make use of query routing.
sections.plainLanguage: Each server owns a fixed set of data, and a search normally stops at the server that received it. Indexing lets that server point the search onward by answering with a referral to another server. The referral is only a hint, because an index is a summary of the data rather than a copy of it.

sections.title: The CIP Index Object
sections.content:
The core of the protocol is the index object, which has two parts: a header and a payload. The header holds the metadata needed to process the object and make use of it. The payload holds the index itself.

Three header fields matter here. The type of the index object selects one of the distinct index object specifications, which define exactly how the index blocks are to be created, parsed and used to facilitate query routing. The DSI, or Dataset Identifier, uniquely identifies the dataset from which the index was created; the RFC's glossary says it is chosen from any part of the ISO/CCITT OID space. The Base-URI holds the URI or URIs that form the basis of any referral generated from this index block, and it is also an input to index aggregation, because the aggregation algorithm constrains what may be merged with it.

The payload is opaque to CIP itself. Its format is defined exclusively by the index object specification associated with the object's MIME type, and specifications on how to parse and use it are published separately. This abstraction is what lets the same machinery carry indices for many application domains.
sections.plainLanguage: The unit of information that servers pass around is an index object. It has a header that says what kind of index it is, which dataset it describes and where that data lives, plus a payload holding the index itself. CIP does not look inside the payload, so the same machinery can carry very different kinds of index.

sections.title: Passing Indices Through a Mesh
sections.content:
A CIP mesh is a set of CIP servers that pass indices of the same type among themselves. A mesh is typically arranged in a hierarchical tree fashion, with servers nearer the root holding larger and more comprehensive indices, but a mesh is explicitly allowed to have lateral links, and more than one part of the mesh may have the properties of a root. Administrators are encouraged to avoid loops but are not obliged to maintain a strict tree structure.

All indices passed in a given mesh are assumed to be of the same type, governed by the same index object specification. It may be possible to build gateways between meshes carrying different index objects, but that process is undefined and outside the scope of this specification. A server that receives an index of a type it does not understand may pass that index forward untouched; a server that decides not to accept unknown indices should return an appropriate error message to the server sending it.

Index passing should run as a parallel and possibly lower-priority job next to the server's primary work of answering queries. The RFC states the distinction directly: queries are answered and referrals are sent via the native data access protocol, while index objects are transferred by the alternative means this document defines.

Two ways of moving indices are described. In a polling relationship, the polled server holds the data of interest and generates the index, and the polling server collects the generated index. The polled server notifies the polling server when it has a new index that might interest it; the polling server may pick the index up immediately or schedule a job to collect it later, and it may also request a new index at any time. In an index pushing relationship, a server simply sends the index to a peer when it sees fit, and the receiver may refuse it, accept it and silently discard it, accept only portions of it, or accept it without question. Pushing is intended for simple leaf nodes that want their index available to the mesh without implementing the complete CIP transaction protocol.

Index passing operations take place across reliable transport mechanisms, including both TCP connections and Internet mail messages. The precise mechanisms are described in the transport document.
sections.plainLanguage: The servers that exchange indices form a mesh, usually shaped like a hierarchy where the top servers hold the most complete summaries. A server can ask a peer for its index, which is polling, or simply send it, which is pushing. Index traffic is separate from client traffic: clients keep using the server's ordinary data protocol, while indices move by CIP's own exchanges.

sections.title: Aggregating Index Objects
sections.content:
A server need not pass every index it holds on unchanged. It may aggregate two or more index objects into a single new one, which reduces redundancy in the index at the cost of longer referral chains.

The premise of index passing is that hints useful for routing survive the lossy compression of a dataset into an index. As more information collects in a resulting index, redundancy creeps back in, and applying the compression again by aggregating objects into one may be useful. Aggregation must not compromise the ability to route queries while avoiding excessive numbers of missed results: the acceptable likelihood of false negatives has to be established on a per-application-domain basis, and it is controlled by the granularity of the index and the aggregation rules defined for it by the particular specification.

In a multi-protocol application domain, such as a directory service, the problem is harder. The fundamental issue is to avoid forcing a referral chain to pass through part of the mesh that does not support the protocol by which the client made its query. If that happens, the client loses access to any hits beyond that point in the chain, which is a failure of query routing. Server managers may also decline to aggregate for performance reasons, because longer referral chains mean more transactions for the client, more delay, more load and more bandwidth.

Two rules control how a server formulates its outgoing indices. First, an index server may pass any of the index objects in its local index and its in-bound indices through unchanged to polling servers. Second, if and only if all three of the following are true, an index server can aggregate two or more index objects into a single new index object: each object to be aggregated covers exactly the same set of protocols, as defined by the scheme component of the Base-URIs in each index object; the index server supports every one of the data access protocols represented by those Base-URIs; and the specification for the index object type explicitly defines the aggregation operation. The resulting object must have Base-URIs characteristic of the local server for each protocol it supports, and the outgoing objects should have the DSI of the local server.
sections.plainLanguage: A server can merge the indices it holds into one. That saves bandwidth but makes the client follow longer chains of referrals, and it can cause the client to miss results that an unmerged index would have found. Merging is only allowed when the merged indices cover the same set of protocols, the server supports all of them, and the index type's own specification defines how to merge them.

sections.title: Navigating the Mesh and Following Referrals
sections.content:
CIP decides when a referral should be issued and generates it, while the server's native protocol carries it to the client. A referral is made when a search against the index objects held by the server shows that there may be hits available in one of the datasets those objects represent. If more than one index object indicates that a referral must be generated to a given dataset, the server should generate only one referral to that dataset, because the client may not be able to detect duplicates.

Whatever the protocol, the baseline contents of a referral are the same. At least a DSI and a URI must be returned. The DSI is the one associated with the dataset that caused the hit, and it must be presented to the client so that it can avoid referral loops. The Base-URI parameter that travels along with index objects provides the other required part. The additional information in the Base-URI may be needed by the server receiving the referred query: an LDAP server, for example, needs a base X.500 distinguished name from which to search, so it sends that name with the index object and the referral passes it back to the client. A human-readable DSI-Description header may also be sent, and should be included in referrals when it is available.

Each data access protocol that uses CIP needs a clearly defined set of rules mapping queries in the native protocol to searches against an index object, and the RFC notes the scaling difficulty this creates: for N protocols and M data domains there would be N x M mappings. In practice some access protocols are wholly unsuited to some data domains, and the index object specification must state the application- and protocol-specific actions it needs.

The client does the travelling. The simplest client presents referrals to the user in a raw, ready-to-reuse form without following them: one Whois++ client that talks to the user through a web-based form simply makes referrals into HTML hypertext links, with the hostname, port and query encoded by the HTML forms GET encoding rules, so following a link runs the search on the new host. A client that follows every referral must use some form of mesh traversal algorithm, because the mesh is an interconnected graph that may have cycles and could otherwise send referrals round and round forever. The Whois++ algorithm documented in RFC 1914 works unchanged with CIP once its handle is read as a DSI. The entry point also matters: using a single root node that every client must connect to does not scale, so clients should start at a reasonably well connected local server, and if no match is found there, ask that server who polls it.
sections.plainLanguage: The server decides when a referral is needed and puts it into the client's own protocol. A referral names the dataset and the address of the server holding it. The client then follows referrals itself, and it has to avoid going round in circles, because the mesh can contain loops.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC names three levels at which security comes into play. Indexing information can leak undesirable amounts of proprietary information unless it is carefully controlled. The CIP protocol itself requires external security services to operate in a safe manner. And CIP can be used to propagate false information.

On the first point, a data publisher taking part in a mesh is exporting a summary of the asset that is its prime asset, so the index must be designed to protect the database while still providing a useful synopsis of the data. The risk of reverse engineering a database from the index exported from it must be kept to a level consistent with the value of the data and the need for fine-grained indexing. Legal considerations about what data may be collected and shared also apply.

On the third point, the insertion of false data into a mesh can be used as part of an attack. Depending on the type of mesh and the aggregation algorithms, an index can selectively prune parts of a mesh. Because CIP is used to discover information, it will be the target for the advertisement of false information. The RFC is explicit about the limit: CIP does not provide a method for trusting the data that it contains.
sections.plainLanguage: Sharing an index can reveal more about a database than its owner wants, so indexes need careful design. Worse, a server that puts false data into a mesh can prune parts of it or send searchers to the wrong place. CIP has no way to check whether the data it carries is true.
